name: Sillage and projection

card.summary: Two ways of describing a fragrance's reach, how far it radiates around you and the trail it leaves, used to pick scents that make a noticeable but pleasant impression.
card.note: Perceived strength varies with skin chemistry, application and the nose of the observer.

quick.overview:
Sillage is the trail of scent a person leaves behind as they move; projection is how far a fragrance radiates around the wearer while they stay still. Fragrance enthusiasts track both, alongside longevity, to choose scents that register on others without overwhelming them.

The payoff for appearance is presentation: scent is part of the overall impression someone makes, and these terms give a vocabulary for choosing and wearing it. Retailer and enthusiast sources, rather than controlled research, supply most of the descriptions.
quick.how: People test a fragrance on skin or a blotter and note how far away it can be smelled and how long it lingers, sometimes asking a friend to judge. Higher oil concentrations such as eau de parfum and extrait are generally linked to longer wear and stronger presence, though labels are loosely regulated. Number of sprays and application spot change the effect.
quick.risks: Strong projection can bother people nearby, and fragrance can trigger sensitivities or allergies; some workplaces and venues are scent-restricted. Your own nose can tire, so you may stop noticing the scent you wear.

lead: In perfumery, sillage is the trail of scent left behind by a person wearing perfume; the word is French for the wake of a boat [1]. Projection describes how far the scent reaches around the wearer while staying relatively still, and longevity is how long it stays noticeable [2].

Enthusiasts use these terms to choose fragrances that stand out for good reasons: a scent that projects well draws attention, while one that stays close to the skin is more personal. Appearance-focused communities treat fragrance as one more part of the overall impression.
Descriptions of these terms come from perfume retailers and fragrance writers; no clinical studies on sillage or projection as such are cited here.

chain: Adjust how many sprays and where
Scent radiates and trails at a chosen level
Wearer leaves a noticeable, pleasant impression
angle.text: People use sillage and projection to compare fragrances and decide how strongly a scent should announce them, as part of grooming.

paras: Sillage comes from the French for wake [1]. A fragrance writer separates three qualities: longevity (how long a scent is noticeable), projection (reach while still) and sillage (the trail while moving) [2].

The same source reports that skin chemistry, hydration, temperature, airflow and nose fatigue all affect results, and recommends consistent testing such as logging wear time at intervals, having a friend judge distance, or using a control blotter [2]. Higher oil concentrations are generally linked to longer wear and stronger presence, but the labels are not strictly regulated [2].
